subtopics.title: Continue linear sequences
subtopics.exposition: The common difference is the difference between any term and the term before it. Sequences with a common difference are called linear sequences. In general, the common difference is d = T_n - T_(n-1). To calculate the common difference, find the difference between any term and the previous term. For the sequence 10; 7; 4; 1, the common difference between the first two terms is found as d = T_2 - T_1 = 7 - 10 = -3. Check the common difference with another two terms (for 10; 7; 4; 1, d = T_4 - T_3 = 1 - 4 = -3) and see that d is constant. For 1; 4; 7; 10; ... there is a difference of 3 between successive terms, and the pattern is continued by adding 3 to the previous term. For 13; 8; 3; -2; ... the difference is -5, and the pattern is continued by adding -5 to the previous term, which is the same as subtracting 5 from it. To continue a figure pattern, make a table of the number of tables against the number of people seated to see if a pattern forms. To describe a figure pattern, see how much the number of people increases for each table added (here 2 more each time, starting from 4), which gives the pattern 4; 6; 8; 10; ... and the next terms. The common difference is denoted by d.

subtopics.title: Identify terms using T_n
subtopics.exposition: A sequence is an ordered list of items, usually numbers. Each item which makes up a sequence is called a term. The first term of a sequence is written T_1. The fourth term of a sequence is written T_4. The tenth term of a sequence is written T_10. The general term is often expressed as the nth term and is written as T_n.

subtopics.title: Find the general formula
subtopics.exposition: A sequence does not have to follow a pattern but, when it does, we can write down the general formula to calculate any term. For the linear sequence 1; 3; 5; 7; 9; ... the nth term is given by the general formula T_n = 2n - 1. The difference between the successive terms is always the coefficient of n in the formula; this is called a common difference. For sequences with a common difference, the general formula will always be of the form T_n = dn + c, where d is the difference between each term and c is some constant. To find a general formula, find the relationship between the position of a term and its value; the formula then matches the pattern and gives any term in the sequence. To find the general formula for a list of terms such as 6; 1; -4; -9; ..., set the terms out in a table. In the table for 6; 1; -4; -9; ..., the terms are written as 6 - 0x5, 6 - 1x5, 6 - 2x5, 6 - 3x5 and so the nth term is written as 6 - (n - 1) x 5. For a picture pattern, make a table of the number of tables, n, against the number of people seated, and write the pattern for each term. From the table (4 = 4+2(0), 6 = 4+2(1), 8 = 4+2(2), ...), the number of people seated at n tables is T_n = 4 + 2(n - 1). In the data plans table, the costs 135, 150, 165 are written as 120 plus 1, 2, 3 lots of 15, which is how the pattern is observed. Use the observed pattern to determine the general formula: the price of n GB of data is T_n = 120 + 15(n - 1).

subtopics.title: Use the general formula
subtopics.exposition: You can check a general formula by substituting values of n into the formula. To calculate a required term, substitute its position for n in the general formula: for T_n = 4 + 2(n - 1), T_12 = 4 + 2(12 - 1) = 4 + 22 = 26. To find how many tables are needed to seat 20 people, put T_n = 20 in the general formula and solve for n. To solve for n, expand the brackets (20 = 4 + 2n - 2), collect the numbers (18 = 2n) and divide by the coefficient of n to get n = 9. To determine the cost of a 30 GB plan, find T_n if n = 30, using the general formula. Substituting n = 30 into T_n = 120 + 15(n - 1) gives T_30 = 120 + 15(29) = 555. To find n when the value of a term is given, set T_n equal to that value (520 = 120 + 15(n - 1)), expand, simplify (520 = 105 + 15n, then 405 = 15n) and solve for n, giving n = 27. From n = 27 the book concludes it is cheaper to purchase the unlimited data plan if he uses more than 27 GB per month.

claims.claim: A sequence is an ordered list of items, usually numbers.
Each item which makes up a sequence is called a term.
The first term of a sequence is written T_1.
The fourth term of a sequence is written T_4.
The tenth term of a sequence is written T_10.
The general term is often expressed as the nth term and is written as T_n.
It is important to note the difference between n and T_n: n can be compared to a place holder indicating the position of the term in the sequence.
T_n is the value of the place held by n, so the position n and the value T_n are different things.
The common difference is the difference between any term and the term before it.
The common difference is denoted by d.
To calculate the common difference, find the difference between any term and the previous term.
For the sequence 10; 7; 4; 1, the common difference between the first two terms is found as d = T_2 - T_1 = 7 - 10 = -3.
Check the common difference with another two terms (for 10; 7; 4; 1, d = T_4 - T_3 = 1 - 4 = -3) and see that d is constant.
In general, the common difference is d = T_n - T_(n-1).
The common difference is the later term minus the earlier term, not the other way round: for example d = T_2 - T_1, not T_1 - T_2.
For 1; 4; 7; 10; ... there is a difference of 3 between successive terms, and the pattern is continued by adding 3 to the previous term.
For 13; 8; 3; -2; ... the difference is -5, and the pattern is continued by adding -5 to the previous term, which is the same as subtracting 5 from it.
Sequences with a common difference are called linear sequences.
To continue a figure pattern, make a table of the number of tables against the number of people seated to see if a pattern forms.
To describe a figure pattern, see how much the number of people increases for each table added (here 2 more each time, starting from 4), which gives the pattern 4; 6; 8; 10; ... and the next terms.
A sequence does not have to follow a pattern but, when it does, we can write down the general formula to calculate any term.
For the linear sequence 1; 3; 5; 7; 9; ... the nth term is given by the general formula T_n = 2n - 1.
To find a general formula, find the relationship between the position of a term and its value; the formula then matches the pattern and gives any term in the sequence.
To find the general formula for a list of terms such as 6; 1; -4; -9; ..., set the terms out in a table.
In the table for 6; 1; -4; -9; ..., the terms are written as 6 - 0x5, 6 - 1x5, 6 - 2x5, 6 - 3x5 and so the nth term is written as 6 - (n - 1) x 5.
The difference between the successive terms is always the coefficient of n in the formula; this is called a common difference.
For sequences with a common difference, the general formula will always be of the form T_n = dn + c, where d is the difference between each term and c is some constant.
For a picture pattern, make a table of the number of tables, n, against the number of people seated, and write the pattern for each term.
From the table (4 = 4+2(0), 6 = 4+2(1), 8 = 4+2(2), ...), the number of people seated at n tables is T_n = 4 + 2(n - 1).
There may be variations in how you think of a picture pattern; viewing the study table as 1 + 2n + 1 gives 2n + 2, and your formula for T_n will still be correct.
In the data plans table, the costs 135, 150, 165 are written as 120 plus 1, 2, 3 lots of 15, which is how the pattern is observed.
Use the observed pattern to determine the general formula: the price of n GB of data is T_n = 120 + 15(n - 1).
You can check a general formula by substituting values of n into the formula.
To calculate a required term, substitute its position for n in the general formula: for T_n = 4 + 2(n - 1), T_12 = 4 + 2(12 - 1) = 4 + 22 = 26.
To find how many tables are needed to seat 20 people, put T_n = 20 in the general formula and solve for n.
To solve for n, expand the brackets (20 = 4 + 2n - 2), collect the numbers (18 = 2n) and divide by the coefficient of n to get n = 9.
To determine the cost of a 30 GB plan, find T_n if n = 30, using the general formula.
Substituting n = 30 into T_n = 120 + 15(n - 1) gives T_30 = 120 + 15(29) = 555.
To find n when the value of a term is given, set T_n equal to that value (520 = 120 + 15(n - 1)), expand, simplify (520 = 105 + 15n, then 405 = 15n) and solve for n, giving n = 27.
From n = 27 the book concludes it is cheaper to purchase the unlimited data plan if he uses more than 27 GB per month.
